projects.title: 6 Degrees of Freedom Robotic Arm
projects.description: A custom-built 6-degree-of-freedom robotic arm engineered from scratch to test advanced kinematics and motor control systems.Tech Stack: SolidWorks, C++, Numpy, Matplotlib, Closed-Loop Control• Designed and assembled a 6-axis robotic arm with a 0.5kg payload capacity, optimizing torque transmission and selecting specific off-the-shelf actuators to ensure stable lifting.• Implemented Inverse Kinematics (IK) algorithms to dynamically calculate joint angles, enabling precise end-effector positioning in 3D space.• Programmed a closed-loop control system for stepper motors, tuning custom acceleration profiles to eliminate mechanical judder and achieve smooth point-to-point motion.

projects.title: Clinical Prior Authorization RAG Pipeline
projects.description: A RAG pipeline that automates clinical data extraction from unstructured EHR notes into schema-validated Prior Authorization JSON.Tech Stack: Python, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemini Embeddings, Pydantic, NumPy• Built a RAG pipeline that chunks raw EHR text (500-char windows, 100-char overlap), embeds via Gemini's embedding API, and retrieves the most clinically relevant context across 4 patient files using multi-query cosine similarity.• Designed a Pydantic-enforced extraction layer powered by Gemini 2.5 Flash that converts unstructured clinical notes — including OCR artifacts, inconsistent abbreviations, and duplicates — into schema-validated JSON with null-safe graceful failure on missing data.• Engineered multi-query retrieval across diagnosis, failed medications, and lab values with chunk deduplication, enabling structured PA field extraction from messy provider notes that would typically require 15+ minutes of manual clinical staff review per patient.

projects.title: Hawking.ai - EMG Communication Platform
projects.description: An autonomous communication platform designed to transform raw biological signals into context-aware, conversational-speed speech.Tech Stack: Ganglion Board (LSL), FastAPI, React, Gemini 2.0 Flash, ElevenLabs• Engineered an EMG-based communication platform that translates 3 discrete biosignals into semantic grid navigation, boosting user speech rates to 25 WPM (compared to traditional 1-2 WPM limits).• Built a FastAPI WebSocket server integrated with Gemini 2.0 Flash to process real-time sentence predictions, achieving sub-250ms latency for fluid, conversational-speed text generation.• Integrated the ElevenLabs API into a React/TypeScript frontend to synthesize custom biological voices from 10-second audio samples, restoring personal vocal identity for the user.

projects.title: Neuroplay - BCI Gaming Interface
projects.description: An interactive gaming interface controlled entirely by brain activity, built to explore non-invasive BCI applications.Tech Stack: OpenBCI, PyTorch, Signal Processing (FFT):• Engineered an EEG-controlled gaming system using an OpenBCI Ganglion to decode SSVEP and motor-imagery, enabling hands-free gameplay.• Built a signal processing pipeline using Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) and bandpass filters to isolate alpha and beta waves, successfully reducing raw noise and improving signal clarity.• Trained a custom PyTorch neural network to classify 4-channel signals, establishing a 70% baseline accuracy on test data for real-time inference.• Designing a dry-electrode headset configuration that minimized impedance and motion artifacts, maintaining signal integrity during active gaming sessions.

I tried to reverse-engineer the Tesla Optimus wrist for a 6DOF robotic arm. I learned very quickly why that team is so smart. I spent the last 8 weeks figuring out the entire stack, from CAD to code. Here is the breakdown of the build: The Design (SolidWorks & Plastic): Designed the mechanical assembly in SolidWorks. The gap between simulation and reality is humbling. I learned that "theoretical fit" usually means "grab the sandpaper." The Code (The "Math" Phase): Moving from theory to hardware involved significant technical hurdles. I had to write the firmware in Arduino and build the robotics software from scratch. The biggest headache: Resolving singularities in the inverse kinematics (preventing the math from breaking and the arm from locking up) took rounds of debugging. The Hardware (Fighting Physics): You don't realize how much you don't know until you have to troubleshoot in real-time. Spent days mitigating PWM jitter just to get the servos to hold a stable position without shaking. The Future (Tesla & BCI): Currently working on a wrist design inspired by the Tesla Optimus and a custom 3-finger gripper. Next Phase: Transitioning into biomedical applications. I’m going to hook this up to my OpenBCI Ganglion Board to translate EEG signals into gripper commands. Building this reminded me that the fastest way to learn isn't reading the textbook, it's breaking things and fixing them. I haven’t finalized my Summer 2026 internship yet. If you need an engineer who can handle the full stack from Mechanical Design to Python, let’s chat. 🫡 #Robotics #UWaterloo #SystemsDesign #BCI #Mechatronics #Engineering #6DOF ...more

This weekend, we built a voice for those who have lost theirs. Stephen Hawking was limited to speaking at roughly one word per minute. Technology has improved since then, but accessibility hasn't kept pace.This weekend at NexHacks , my team and I built 𝗛𝗮𝘄𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗔𝗜 to close that gap. Using EMG signals and Generative AI, we engineered a high-fidelity neuro-linguistic interface that enables motor-impaired users to communicate at 25 words per minute, an order of magnitude faster than traditional assistive systems, restoring genuine agency rather than merely enabling output. 𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗶𝘁 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝘀 Users communicate via minimal, intentional muscle activations (Right, Down, Select) captured through EMG and mapped onto a semantic grid. Raw signals are "denoised", low-pass filtered, baseline-corrected, and personalized using per-user activation thresholds to reliably separate intent from noise. These commands are streamed in real time to Gemini 2.0 Flash, which predicts intended words using conversational context rather than character-by-character input, and spoken aloud via ElevenLabs, which clones the user’s original voice. The result is not just faster text entry, but a conversational interface that restores agency by translating intent directly into natural speech. 𝗨𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗵𝗼𝗼𝗱: The system runs on a low-latency, event-driven architecture designed to operate in real time. EMG signals are captured via OpenBCI Ganglion over LSL, processed for intent detection, and routed through a FastAPI + WebSockets backend that coordinates inference, prediction, and audio output. Everything is containerized with Docker to ensure reproducibility and deployment readiness. Latency was treated as a first-class constraint, anything that introduced perceptible delay was redesigned or removed. 𝗧𝗲𝗰𝗵 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗰𝗸 Gemini 2.0 Flash — real-time contextual word generation Eleven Labs — voice cloning and natural speech output WoodWide AI — EMG denoising and intent detection OpenBCI Ganglion + LSL — real-time EMG signal capture FastAPI + WebSockets — low-latency system orchestration React + TypeScript — responsive, minimal UI Docker — production-ready deployment Huge props to the team Aditya Mahes Ryan Zhou Vanshdeep Sehrawat for grinding through the weekend to make this happen. 🔗 Devpost: https://lnkd.in/e9uYGrkB 🔗 Video demo: https://lnkd.in/etadx4gu #GenerativeAI #NeuroTech #Hackathon #CMU #OpenBCI ...more

Last weekend, we didn't just participate in the SWARM Hackathon...we took 3rd place with the development of one of the largest functional robot swarms in the competition! Our challenge: Design and build a swarm of autonomous robots capable of mimicking natural collective behaviour. Throughout the weekend our team: - Assembled and programmed a coordinated robot swarm from scratch -Integrated custom PCB boards, 3D-printed chassis, and embedded systems -Developed swarm intelligence in ROS1 using Python -Enabled dynamic communication and multi-agent coordination Our Approach: We engineered a small-scale swarm capable of distributed sensing and communication, with each robot designed to operate semi-autonomously while contributing to a shared objective. The vision: a collective system capable of exploring unknown terrains more efficiently than any single rover could. The Reality Check? Let’s just say our swarm had… commitment issues. Despite endless hours of debugging, soldering, and testing, our robots decided to move one at a time — a polite but not-so-effective formation. Still, the experience was nothing short of amazing. From troubleshooting PCB connections to fine-tuning our ROS nodes, every challenge taught us something new about robotics, systems integration, and teamwork under pressure. Huge thanks to my incredible teammates, for your relentless drive, creativity, and humour throughout the chaos! We may not have built the perfect swarm (yet), but we built the foundation for something greater. Next time, our swarm will actually swarm. #SWARMHackathon #Robotics #Engineering #Hackathon #SwarmRobotics #Innovation #Teamwork #UWaterloo #LearningByDoing #STEM ...more

A 60yr old soldering iron, wires stripped from old electronics, 1 paper clip, 3 pen springs, a couple circuitry pieces, and an Arduino. That’s all you need to make a pulse oximeter. For the past couple weeks I have been modeling, 3D printing, soldering, building, and calibrating my own pulse oximeter, which I am proud to say can monitor your blood oxygen and heart rate with 95% accuracy! Using a red and infrared LED, a photodiode measures light absorbance depending on the oxygen saturation and blood flow. The oxygenated vs deoxygenated hemoglobin in your blood absorb red and infrared light differently, which allows the device to estimate blood oxygen saturation, and the pulsatile blood flow allows it to determine heart rate. Simple enough, right? While it may seem technically simple, the most challenging part (and most valuable lesson) wasn’t simply getting the device to work. It was the continual iterations and problem solving to make the mechanical design, software, and technical pieces all work in tandem. During the project, I went through four different designs, two sets of hardware, and was constantly adjusting the system because the real engineering challenge wasn’t it’s creation, it was making the system reliable and repeatable. In the end, this project took me from someone who had never touched a soldering iron and couldn’t tell the difference between a transistor vs resistor, to someone who troubleshooted circuits and code to make a biomedical device on her own. And this is just the beginning.

Neuromorphic (YC S26) is building embodiment-agnostic robot brains that make any robot fast to deploy and easy to manage through natural interfaces like Slack, email, and phone. Starting with wet labs! Deploying robots today is slow, expensive, and engineering-intensive. Most systems are built around a specific body and environment, making them difficult to adapt when the task or hardware changes. Programming and managing them also requires specialized technical knowledge, keeping automation out of many physical industries. Neuromorphic packages sensors, compute, and software into a “brain” that can be attached to different robot bodies. An onboard LLM orchestrator turns natural-language instructions into workflows made up of reusable robotic skills, such as navigating, picking up an object, opening a refrigerator, or inspecting an area. Sensor-based safety loops monitor every action to ensure reliable execution. Within a week of the initial conversation, the team signed a contract with a leading biotechnology company and deployed a robot in their wet lab, capable of operating autonomously 24/7 and already completing over 1500 tasks. Founders Cem Seref Toker and Ege Doğanay were teammates doing high school robotics (FIRST Robotics Competition) when they reached out to Vatan Aksoy Tezer for mentorship and robotics advice. Together, they spent 3 years winning robotics competitions and have kept close ties ever since, before founding Neuromorphic together. Neuromorphic’s goal is to make deploying a robot as straightforward as onboarding a new employee: show it around, tell it what to do, and have it start working from day one. Are you operating in a wet lab, biotech, or physical industry? You can reach out to Cem, Ege, and Vatan through founders@neuromorphic.vision to get more robots next to you! Congrats on the launch, Cem, Ege, and Vatan! 🚀 https://lnkd.in/gGhPGzsx
